# quantum-safe-ts: full reference for LLMs and coding agents

quantum-safe-ts is a TypeScript/JavaScript library for hybrid post-quantum cryptography. A Rust core is compiled to
WebAssembly and wrapped in a typed API. It is byte-compatible with the Python library quantum-safe-py.

STATUS (as stated by the project): pre-1.0, experimental, NOT independently audited, NOT FIPS 140-3 / CMVP
validated. NIST ACVP known-answer results are conformance evidence, not a validation. JavaScript and WebAssembly runtimes
give no constant-time guarantee. It is not recommended for protecting real secrets until an independent review is published.

Snippets in fenced blocks labelled `ts test` are executed by this package's test suite against the built WASM, so they are
known to run.

## 1. When to use it, and when not to

Use it when you need: hybrid (classical + post-quantum) encryption or signatures with typed errors; key serialization (CBOR,
PEM, JWK); PQC JWTs; an Argon2id master key; or data that must interoperate with quantum-safe-py.

Do not use it when: you only need a raw ML-KEM/ML-DSA primitive (use WebCrypto in Node >= 24.7 / Chromium, or
@noble/post-quantum); you need a FIPS 140-3 validated module (none that we know of is); or you need TLS (platforms already
negotiate X25519MLKEM768, RFC 10024).

## 2. Install and initialise

`npm install quantum-safe-ts`

- Node.js 20+ (tested on 20, 22, 24; ESM and CommonJS): the WASM initialises on import. `await init()` is a harmless no-op.
- Browsers, Deno, Bun, edge runtimes: call `await init()` once before any other call. The WASM is embedded; no bundler plugin is
  needed (verified with Vite, webpack 5, esbuild, Next.js, SvelteKit).
- Cloudflare Workers forbid compiling WASM from bytes: `import wasm from 'quantum-safe-ts/quantum_safe_wasm_bg.wasm'; await init({ wasm });`
- Chrome MV3 extensions: the extension CSP must include `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`.
- Calling any API before initialisation throws `NotInitializedError`.
- Bundle size: the default entry embeds the WebAssembly (about 600 KiB gzipped). `quantum-safe-ts/slim` has the same API and no embedded WebAssembly: `await init({ wasm: fetch(url) })` with `quantum-safe-ts/wasm` as the file.

## 3. Algorithms (names are wire-visible identifiers; never change them)

KEM suites (`kemSuites()`): `X25519+ML-KEM-512`, `X25519+ML-KEM-768` (default), `X25519+ML-KEM-1024`, `P-256+ML-KEM-512`,
`P-256+ML-KEM-768`, `X-Wing`, and pure `ML-KEM-512`, `ML-KEM-768`, `ML-KEM-1024`.
Signature suites (`sigSuites()`): `Ed25519+ML-DSA-44`, `Ed25519+ML-DSA-65` (default hybrid), `Ed25519+ML-DSA-87`,
`P-256+ML-DSA-44`, `P-256+ML-DSA-65`, `ML-DSA-44`, `ML-DSA-65`, `ML-DSA-87`, and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205): `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s`,
`SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f`, `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-192s`, `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-192f`, `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256s`, `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f`,
`SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s`, `SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f`, `SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s`, `SLH-DSA-SHA2-192f`, `SLH-DSA-SHA2-256s`, `SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f`.
quantum-safe-py reads all except `X-Wing` and the nine SLH-DSA sets it does not list (only SHAKE-128s/128f/256s are shared).
Signature format v2 (no prefix; read and written by quantum-safe-py 0.3.2+, not by 0.3.0; ML-DSA half signs a wrapped message `M2` under the FIPS 204 context `quantum-safe-sig-v2`, so it is NOT a standard signature over your message; keys tagged `-v2`): `ML-DSA-44-v2`, `ML-DSA-65-v2`, `ML-DSA-87-v2`,
`Ed25519+ML-DSA-44-v2`, `Ed25519+ML-DSA-65-v2`, `Ed25519+ML-DSA-87-v2`, `P-256+ML-DSA-44-v2`, `P-256+ML-DSA-65-v2`. Prefer v2 unless a quantum-safe-py older than 0.3.2 must verify the signature (the default of `easy` stays `Ed25519+ML-DSA-65` until the next minor release).

Choosing: default hybrids are NIST category 3. CNSA 2.0 requires ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87: use pure `ML-KEM-1024` (`cnsa2.kem()`;
hybrid is optional under CNSA 2.0) and `ML-DSA-87` (`Ed25519+ML-DSA-87` from `cnsa2.hybridSign()` has the right parameter set but reports `partial`: a hybrid is outside what CNSA 2.0 prescribes), and see section 9 for what CNSA 2.0 still lacks. For data
other ecosystems must read, use `X-Wing` (draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem) and `StandardJwt` (RFC 9964) instead of the
quantum-safe-py-compatible constructions.

Streaming (experimental, TypeScript-only): `sealStream(publicKey, source, { aad, chunkSize })` and `openStream(secretKey, source, { expectedAad })` take and yield `Uint8Array` pieces (async generators); a truncated, reordered or modified stream throws and stops. See the streaming guide.

## 3b. Easy layer (shortest path, nothing to free)

```ts test
import { easy } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

const keys = easy.generateEncryptionKeys(); // { publicKey, secretKey, algorithm }: PEM strings, default X25519+ML-KEM-768
const sealed = easy.encrypt(keys.publicKey, 'hello', { aad: 'ctx' }); // Uint8Array (CBOR SealedMessage)
if (new TextDecoder().decode(easy.decrypt(keys.secretKey, sealed)) !== 'hello') throw new Error('round trip');

const signer = easy.generateSigningKeys(); // default Ed25519+ML-DSA-65
const signed = easy.sign(signer.secretKey, 'doc', { context: 'docs-v1' }); // Uint8Array (CBOR SignedMessage)
if (new TextDecoder().decode(easy.verify(signer.publicKey, signed, { context: 'docs-v1' })) !== 'doc') throw new Error('verify');
```

- `easy` wraps the class API and frees every WASM object before returning. Keys are PEM strings, which quantum-safe-py reads and writes too.
- Trade-off: a secret key held as a string lives in the JavaScript heap and cannot be wiped by the library. Use the class API with `using` when that matters.
- `verify` returns the signed message and throws `VerificationError` unless the signature is valid AND its context equals `options.context` (default empty).
- `encrypt`/`decrypt` use the quantum-safe-py-compatible envelope; for the CNSA 2.0 profile use `cnsa2.kem()` with `Envelope`.

## 4. Key encapsulation

```ts test
import { HybridKEM, KEM, utf8, equalBytes } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

const kem = new HybridKEM('X25519+ML-KEM-768');
using pair = kem.generateKeyPair(); // `using` frees (wipes) the secret key at scope exit
const { ciphertext, sharedSecret } = kem.encapsulate(pair.publicKey); // sender
using recovered = kem.decapsulate(pair.secretKey, ciphertext); // key holder
if (!equalBytes(recovered.exportBytes(), sharedSecret.exportBytes())) throw new Error('mismatch');
const sessionKey = sharedSecret.deriveKey(32, utf8('myapp-session-v1')); // HKDF-SHA256, no salt
sharedSecret.free();
const pure = new KEM('ML-KEM-768'); // pure ML-KEM: not recommended for new deployments (except ML-KEM-1024 in the CNSA 2.0 profile)
if (pure.algorithm !== 'ML-KEM-768' || sessionKey.length !== 32) throw new Error('unexpected');
```

- `HybridKEM(algorithm = 'X25519+ML-KEM-768')` accepts hybrid names and `X-Wing`. `KEM(algorithm = 'ML-KEM-768')` accepts pure names.
- `encapsulate(publicKey)` returns `{ ciphertext: Uint8Array, sharedSecret: SecretBytes }`.
- `decapsulate(secretKey, ciphertext)` returns `SecretBytes`. ML-KEM uses implicit rejection (FIPS 203): a wrong ciphertext yields a
  different pseudorandom secret instead of an error; the failure appears downstream (for example at AEAD authentication).
  Structurally invalid ciphertexts throw `MalformedCiphertextError`.
- Mixing a key of one algorithm with a KEM of another throws `AlgorithmMismatchError`.

## 5. Envelope (authenticated public-key encryption)

```ts test
import { Envelope, HybridKEM, SealedMessage, DecryptionAuthenticationError, utf8 } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

using pair = new HybridKEM().generateKeyPair();
const sealed = Envelope.seal(utf8('secret'), pair.publicKey, { aad: utf8('item-42') }); // AES-256-GCM under an HKDF key
const plain = Envelope.open(sealed, pair.secretKey); // Uint8Array; call wipe(plain) if sensitive
const wire = sealed.toBytes(); // CBOR, identical to quantum-safe-py SealedMessage.to_bytes()
const again = SealedMessage.fromBytes(wire);
if (again.algorithm !== 'X25519+ML-KEM-768' || plain.length !== 6) throw new Error('unexpected');
try {
  Envelope.open(SealedMessage.fromParts({ ...again, aad: utf8('other') }), pair.secretKey);
  throw new Error('should not open');
} catch (e) {
  if (!(e instanceof DecryptionAuthenticationError)) throw e;
}
```

- `Envelope.seal(plaintext, publicKey, { aad? })`. The AAD is authenticated and stored in clear in the message.
- `Envelope.open(sealed | bytes, secretKey, { expectedAad? })` throws `DecryptionAuthenticationError` for a wrong key, any tampering, or an AAD different from `expectedAad`. The AAD is stored inside the message, so WITHOUT `expectedAad` any AAD opens (anyone holding the public key can seal a message): envelopes are anonymous and do not authenticate the sender; sign separately for that. `easy.decrypt(secretKey, sealed, { aad })` is the same.
- Envelopes require a hybrid key, except pure `ML-KEM-1024`, which produces an envelope v2 (CNSA 2.0 profile: HKDF-SHA-384 + AES-256-GCM,
  also read and written by quantum-safe-py 0.3.2+). Other pure ML-KEM keys throw `UnsupportedAlgorithmError`.
- `SealedMessage` fields: `version`, `algorithm`, `kemCiphertext`, `nonce`, `ciphertext`, `aad`; methods `toBytes`, `toHex`, `inspect`,
  `fromBytes`, `fromHex`, `fromParts`.

## 6. Signatures

```ts test
import { HybridSign, Sign, VerificationError, utf8 } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

const signer = new HybridSign('Ed25519+ML-DSA-65');
using pair = signer.generateKeyPair();
const signed = signer.signWithFingerprint(utf8('contract v3'), pair, { context: utf8('myapp-v1-docs') });
signer.verify(signed, pair.publicKey, { expectedContext: utf8('myapp-v1-docs') }); // throws VerificationError unless BOTH signatures verify AND the context matches
const tampered = Uint8Array.from(signed.message, (b, i) => (i === 0 ? b ^ 1 : b));
try {
  signer.verifyBytes(tampered, signed.signature, pair.publicKey, { context: utf8('myapp-v1-docs') });
  throw new Error('should not verify');
} catch (e) {
  if (!(e instanceof VerificationError)) throw e;
}
const pure = new Sign('ML-DSA-87', { hedged: true });
using p2 = pure.generateKeyPair();
if (!pure.isValid(pure.sign(utf8('x'), p2.secretKey), p2.publicKey)) throw new Error('unexpected');
```

- `sign(message, secretKey, { context?, signerFingerprint? })` returns a `SignedMessage` (`message`, `signature`, `algorithm`, `context`,
  `signerFingerprint`, `signedAt`, `isHybrid`). `message` must be non-empty; `context` is at most 255 bytes.
- Hedged signing (32 random prefix bytes) is the default, as in quantum-safe-py. `verify` throws `VerificationError` with a fixed
  message and no detail about why.
- Verifier settings that are security checks: `verify(signed, publicKey, { expectedContext })` requires the context YOU signed with (default empty; the message's own context is never trusted), and the verifier's `hedged`
  must match the signer's: a hedged verifier (default) requires a 32-byte prefix, `{ hedged: false }` requires none. Without that pinning the prefix/message boundary in the unsigned signature blob could be moved to forge
  signatures on a suffix of a signed message. `easy.verify(publicKey, signed, { context, hedged })` does both.
- Compatibility note: quantum-safe-py's "context" is a message prefix (`len(ctx) || ctx || prefix || message`) with an empty FIPS 204 context.
  A generic ML-DSA verifier will not accept these signatures unless it rebuilds that input.

## 7. JWT

```ts test
import { JWTSigner, JWTVerifier, StandardJwt, HybridSign } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

// quantum-safe-py mode (only quantum-safe-py / quantum-safe-ts can verify these tokens):
using pair = new HybridSign().generateKeyPair();
const token = new JWTSigner(pair, { issuer: 'https://issuer.example' }).sign({ sub: 'user-1' }, { expiresIn: 600 });
const claims = new JWTVerifier(pair.publicKey, { issuer: 'https://issuer.example' }).verify(token);

// Standards mode, RFC 9964 (any compliant JOSE implementation can verify these):
const { publicJwk, privateJwk } = StandardJwt.generateKeyPair('ML-DSA-65', { kid: 'k1' });
const std = StandardJwt.sign({ sub: 'user-1', aud: 'api' }, privateJwk, { expiresIn: 600 });
const ok = StandardJwt.verify(std, publicJwk, { audience: 'api' });
if (claims.sub !== 'user-1' || ok.sub !== 'user-1') throw new Error('unexpected');
```

- Both modes pin the algorithm to the key, reject `alg: "none"` and mismatched `alg`, validate `exp`/`nbf` (30 s skew) and optional `iss`/`aud`.
- Claim failures throw a bare `VerificationError`. Structurally malformed tokens throw `InvalidArgumentError`.
- A private AKP JWK contains the secret seed as a string (inherent to JWK): store it like a secret key.

## 8. Keys, serialization, passwords

```ts test
import { PublicKey, SecretKey, KeyPair, HybridKEM, deriveMasterKey, utf8, toHex } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

using pair = new HybridKEM().generateKeyPair();
const pem = pair.publicKey.toPem(); // QUANTUM SAFE PUBLIC KEY (identical to quantum-safe-py to_pem())
const jwk = pair.publicKey.toJwk(); // kty "AKP"; public keys only (secret keys are never JWK)
const back = PublicKey.fromPem(pem);
if (back.fingerprint() !== pair.publicKey.fingerprint()) throw new Error('fingerprint');
const bundle = pair.toCborBundle(); // contains the secret: protect it
using restored = KeyPair.fromCborBundle(bundle);
if (restored.algorithm !== 'X25519+ML-KEM-768' || jwk.length < 10) throw new Error('unexpected');

using master = await deriveMasterKey('correct horse battery staple', utf8('0123456789abcdef')); // Argon2id
const authKey = master.deriveKey(32, utf8('myapp-auth-v1'));
const vaultKey = master.deriveKey(32, utf8('myapp-vault-v1'));
if (toHex(authKey) === toHex(vaultKey)) throw new Error('subkeys must differ');
```

- Formats: `toCbor`/`fromCbor` (`{v, algo, ms, ktype, key}`), `toPem`/`fromPem`, `toJwk`/`fromJwk` (public only), `fingerprint()` =
  `sha256(algorithm || 0x00 || key)` hex. Parsing rejects public/secret type confusion, version rollback, and payloads over 10 MB.
- `deriveMasterKey(password, salt)`: Argon2id (19 MiB, 2 passes, 1 lane), salt >= 8 bytes (use 16+ random). No Unicode
  normalisation is applied: normalise passwords yourself (for example NFKC). In browsers run it in a Web Worker.

## 9. CNSA 2.0 profile

```ts test
import { cnsa2 } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

const report = cnsa2.report({ kem: 'X25519+ML-KEM-768', signature: 'Ed25519+ML-DSA-65' });
if (report.compliant) throw new Error('the defaults are below CNSA 2.0');
const kem = cnsa2.kem(); // pure ML-KEM-1024: Envelope.seal() then produces envelope v2 (HKDF-SHA-384)
cnsa2.enforce({ kem: kem.algorithm, signature: 'ML-DSA-87' }, { strict: true }); // throws PolicyViolationError below the parameter sets (strict also rejects 'partial' hybrids)
if (!cnsa2.report({ kem: kem.algorithm, includeCodeSigning: false }).compliant) throw new Error('pure ML-KEM-1024 + envelope v2 meets the KEM requirements');
```

CNSA 2.0 mandates ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87, AES-256, SHA-384/512, and LMS/XMSS (SP 800-208) for software/firmware signing.
Selecting the parameter sets is necessary and not sufficient. Known gaps in this library, reported honestly by `cnsa2.report()`:
(1) a hybrid is outside what CNSA 2.0 prescribes (NSA's FAQ: not required, not to be used on NSS mission systems except NSA-specified exceptions), so `X25519+ML-KEM-1024` is `partial`; hybrid
is optional and pure ML-KEM-1024 is compliant; (2) the quantum-safe-py-compatible hybrid combiner and envelope v1 use HKDF-SHA-256 (below
the SHA-384/512 requirement); pure ML-KEM-1024 envelopes (v2) use HKDF-SHA-384; (3) LMS/XMSS are not implemented; (4) compliance for National
Security Systems runs through FIPS 140-3 validated modules and this library is not one.

## 10. Errors

Every error extends `QuantumSafeError` with a stable `code`, a static `hint`, and `toJSON()`. Match with `instanceof` or `code`;
never parse `message`. Hints never contain key material.

Codes: QS_NOT_INITIALIZED, QS_DECAPSULATION_FAILED, QS_DECRYPTION_FAILED, QS_VERIFICATION_FAILED, QS_SIGNING_FAILED,
QS_MALFORMED_KEY, QS_MALFORMED_CIPHERTEXT, QS_MALFORMED_SIGNATURE, QS_ALGORITHM_MISMATCH, QS_HKDF_OUTPUT_TOO_LONG, QS_KDF_FAILED, QS_KEY_PARSE_ERROR,
QS_INCOMPATIBLE_KEY_VERSION, QS_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE, QS_UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT, QS_UNSUPPORTED_ALGORITHM, QS_INVALID_ARGUMENT,
QS_POLICY_VIOLATION, QS_INTERNAL_ERROR (a bug: report it without secret data).

## 11. Memory and secrets

- `SecretKey`, `SecretBytes` (alias `SharedSecret`) and `KeyPair` hold secrets in WASM memory. `free()` (or `using`) zeroizes the owned buffers (copies from argument passing and parsing may remain; see SECURITY.md) via
  Rust zeroization. Use after free throws `InvalidArgumentError`.
- Bytes you copy out (`exportBytes()`, `toCbor()`/`toPem()` of secrets, plaintext from `Envelope.open`) live in the JS heap and cannot
  be wiped by the library: call `wipe(bytes)` when done. `toString()`, `toJSON()` and `util.inspect` never reveal key material.

## 12. Interop recipes

- Python (quantum-safe-py) sealed this envelope: `Envelope.open(SealedMessage.fromBytes(bytesFromPython), SecretKey.fromCbor(keyBytes))`.
  Keys from `to_cbor()`/`to_pem()` load with the matching `fromCbor`/`fromPem`.
- Other ecosystems must read it: use `HybridKEM('X-Wing')` (interoperable with @noble/post-quantum's `ml_kem768_x25519`) and
  `StandardJwt`.

## 13. Tooling for agents

- `npx quantum-safe-audit scan .` (command: `quantum-safe-audit`) finds classical cryptography in a JS/TS project (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, Ed25519, X25519, DSA, DH, weak hashes,
  classical JWT algorithms, embedded private keys), outputs SARIF and CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM, and suggests migrations.
- `npx quantum-safe-mcp` is an MCP server exposing `audit_path`, `list_rules`, `explain_rule`, `recommend_suite` and `explain_error`.
  It is read-only, offline and path-confined.

## 13b. Migration helpers

`Upgrader` adds a fresh post-quantum half to an existing classical key (the classical bytes are kept, packed as `u16 length || classical || pqc`
exactly like quantum-safe-py); `MigrationStateManager` records `classical_only -> hybrid_transition -> pqc_preferred -> pqc_only` transitions over a
store you provide. It does not find classical crypto (use `quantum-safe-audit`) or re-encrypt data.

```ts test
import { MemoryMigrationStore, MigrationStateManager, Upgrader } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

const manager = new MigrationStateManager(new MemoryMigrationStore());
await manager.transition({
  keyId: 'k1', fromState: 'classical_only', toState: 'hybrid_transition', algorithm: 'X25519+ML-KEM-768', actor: 'ci',
});
if ((await manager.getCurrentState('k1')) !== 'hybrid_transition') throw new Error('state');
if (!Upgrader.checkNeedsUpgrade('classical_only')) throw new Error('needs upgrade');
```

- `Upgrader.upgradeKemKey({ classicalSecret, classicalPublic, classicalAlgorithm: 'X25519' | 'P-256', targetPqc })`, `upgradeSigningKey(...)` (Ed25519 | P-256),
  `stripClassicalComponent(keyPair)` (one-way), `checkNeedsUpgrade`, `describeKey`. P-256 secrets are PKCS#8 PEM text bytes; P-256 KEM public keys are the 65-byte
  uncompressed point; P-256 signing public keys are raw 64-byte x||y. A packed hybrid key is not a plain X25519 key: classical-only senders cannot use it.
- Concurrency: each key's history is one document written with one `compareAndSet`. With a store whose `compareAndSet` is atomic, transitions are safe across
  processes and machines (exactly one racer wins). `FileMigrationStore` from `quantum-safe-ts/file-store` (Node only) is a tested single-host implementation.
  Without `compareAndSet` the manager only serialises in-process (`manager.crossProcessSafe` is false).
- quantum-safe-py's migration store uses a different layout (CBOR `<id>_current` / `<id>_history`). `exportToPyStore(manager)` and `importFromPyStore(entries, manager)` convert both ways.

## 14. Choosing, patterns and the rest of the documentation (condensed)

Decision table (full version: /guide/choosing on the documentation site):

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| Encrypt to a public key | `Envelope.seal` with a hybrid key (`HybridKEM`, default `X25519+ML-KEM-768`) |
| CNSA 2.0 parameter sets | `cnsa2.kem()` (pure `ML-KEM-1024`, envelope v2) and `new Sign('ML-DSA-87')`; every hybrid is `partial` |
| Data other (non-Python) ecosystems must decrypt | `X-Wing` |
| Large or streamed data | `sealStream` / `openStream` (experimental) |
| Sign for quantum-safe libraries | `HybridSign` + a `context`, verify with `expectedContext`; prefer `...-v2` when every verifier is quantum-safe-py 0.3.2+ or quantum-safe-ts (the default flips to `-v2` in the next minor release) |
| Tokens only your services verify / any JOSE library verifies | `JWTSigner`/`JWTVerifier` / `StandardJwt` |
| Move keys to post-quantum | `Upgrader` + `MigrationStateManager` |
| Find classical crypto | `quantum-safe-audit` (alias `pqc-audit`), the GitHub Action, or the MCP server (`quantum-safe-mcp`, alias `pqc-mcp`) |

Rules that prevent most mistakes: the verifier states what it expects (`expectedContext`, `expectedAad`), never read them from the message;
always pass a context when signing; sign-then-encrypt (not encrypt-then-sign) for service-to-service messages; never use one key in both signature
formats; derive keys from shared secrets with `deriveKey` and a distinct `info`; `free()` or `using` secret objects and `wipe()` exported copies.

Handling errors from untrusted input:

```ts test
import { easy, QuantumSafeError } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

const keys = easy.generateEncryptionKeys();
function tryOpen(bytes: Uint8Array): string | undefined {
  try {
    return easy.decryptText(keys.secretKey, bytes, { aad: 'inbox-v1' });
  } catch (e) {
    if (QuantumSafeError.is(e) && (e.code === 'QS_DECRYPTION_FAILED' || e.code === 'QS_MALFORMED_CIPHERTEXT' || e.code === 'QS_KEY_PARSE_ERROR')) return undefined;
    throw e; // anything else is a bug: let it surface
  }
}
if (tryOpen(easy.encrypt(keys.publicKey, 'hi', { aad: 'inbox-v1' })) !== 'hi') throw new Error('round trip');
if (tryOpen(new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3])) !== undefined) throw new Error('garbage must be refused');
```

Sign-then-encrypt between two services (full recipe with attacks: /guide/cookbook):

```ts test
import { Envelope, HybridKEM, HybridSign, SignedMessage, utf8 } from 'quantum-safe-ts';

const signer = new HybridSign('Ed25519+ML-DSA-65-v2');
using recipient = new HybridKEM().generateKeyPair();
using sender = signer.generateKeyPair();
const CONTEXT = utf8('orders-v1:A->B');
const wire = Envelope.seal(signer.sign(utf8('shipped'), sender.secretKey, { context: CONTEXT }).toBytes(), recipient.publicKey, { aad: CONTEXT }).toBytes();
const signed = SignedMessage.fromBytes(Envelope.open(wire, recipient.secretKey, { expectedAad: CONTEXT }));
signer.verify(signed, sender.publicKey, { expectedContext: CONTEXT });
if (new TextDecoder().decode(signed.message) !== 'shipped') throw new Error('round trip');
```

Other pages on the site: concepts (hybrid, context/AAD, hedging, the two signature formats, versions), cookbook (7 recipes), Python interop (what crosses,
settings that must match, worked round trips), upgrading, FAQ and troubleshooting, glossary, the audit tool (rules QSJ001-QSJ900, SARIF, CBOM, SBOM,
policy), the GitHub Action, and the MCP server (tools `audit_path`, `list_rules`, `explain_rule`, `recommend_suite`, `explain_error`; resource
`quantum-safe-ts://llms.txt`; read-only, offline, path-confined to `QS_MCP_ROOT`).
